title: Blessed the womb (Luke 11:27–28)
hookLine: a woman praises his mother; he says blessed are they who hear the word and keep it; Catholics see Mary as both

lines: YOUR MOTHER MUST BE SO PROUD.
cards: A son gives a great speech at a wedding, and an aunt in the crowd calls out: your mother must be so proud! It's a compliment to him, routed through her. Something like that happens in Luke.
Jesus is in the middle of a tense argument with people who say he heals by the power of devils. A woman in the crowd can't hold it in. She lifts up her voice and calls out a blessing on his mother.
It's two verses long: what she said, and what he said back.

teach.h: BLESSED IS THE WOMB THAT BORE THEE.
teach.b: Here's her cry in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed is the womb that bore thee, and the paps that gave thee suck." Paps is an old word for breasts.
It's an earthy, motherly blessing, the kind women in that world gave: how happy the mother of such a son.
Jesus answers: "Yea rather, blessed are they who hear the word of God, and keep it." Some people hear that as a brush-off of his mother. Catholics hear something else, and Luke gives the reason.
When the angel came, Mary said be it done to me according to thy word.

At Bethlehem, Luke says, Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart. Elizabeth says to her, blessed art thou that hast believed. And in her own song, Mary says all generations shall call me blessed.
So in Luke, Mary carries both blessings at once: she bore him, and she heard and kept the word.
Augustine said it this way, in his own words: Mary was more blessed in receiving Christ by faith than in conceiving him in the flesh.

teach.h: ONE COULD BEAR HIM; ALL CAN KEEP.
teach.b: Jesus takes a blessing only one woman in history could have, and opens it to everyone listening. Nobody else can be his mother.

teach.h: BLESSED ARE THEY WHO HEAR AND KEEP IT.
teach.b: Anybody can hear and keep. That's why Catholics honor Mary as the first disciple, not only as a mother: she shows what keeping looks like.

how: Catholics read Luke 11:27–28 on some feasts and Saturday Masses of Our Lady, and many pray the rosary as a way of pondering the Gospel's words with Mary.

o: Elizabeth's greeting when Mary came to visit
a prayer said by women who hope for a child
a cry praising his mother, and his answer

p: blessed is the womb that bore thee
yea rather, blessed are they who keep it
kept all these words in her heart
more blessed by faith than by flesh

s: Catholics read Jesus' answer as a put-down of his mother
they read Mary as both: she bore him, and she heard and kept the word.
Luke 11:27–28 has no parallel in the other Gospels.
in Luke, Mary says all generations will call her blessed
in her song, the Magnificat, Luke 1:48.

games.q: a woman in the crowd calls out a blessing on your mother. how does Jesus answer?
o: say rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.
say his mother isn't to be praised.
games.why: he widens the blessing to everyone who hears and keeps the word, and Luke has already shown Mary doing exactly that.

practice: Let one of this week's lines choose you: go in peace, nothing for the journey, no looking back, peace be to this house, knock.
Say it slowly inside a few times, the way Mary pondered, and don't analyze it; just keep it, like a stone in your pocket you keep touching. If you pray, ask to keep it the way she did.

wordCard.voice: Blessed the womb. A woman's cry from the crowd praising Jesus' mother, and his answer: blessed are those who hear the word and keep it, as Mary did. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: blessed, happy, the beatitude word. The woman uses it of the womb, and Jesus answers with it.

carryVoice: Your line: hear and keep it. That's week sixty-six: she loved much, the women who funded him, take nothing, he set his face, the seventy-two, teach us to pray, and the womb. Day four hundred sixty-two, in the books.
